speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to ask the House, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, for unanimous consent to move a motion regarding the inflationary increases in Canada, particularly the increase in fuel oil prices by the oil companies, which the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs agreed yesterday "was obviously inflationary and obviously damaging to the economy". Therefore I ask leave, Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, seconded by the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre, to move the following motion:
That a Standing Committee of the House of Commons to be known as the Standing Committee on Consumer Affairs be established to inquire into and report upon the trends in the cost of living in Canada and factors which may be contributing to changes in the cost of living.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think members would expect me to attempt to respond briefly to some of their questions and to deal, at least in a preliminary way, with some of the very interesting comments they have made in this debate. I thank them for their contributions to it. I am sure we could go into the matters that have been raised so far in the debate in greater detail when this bill is before the standing committee.
The hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. MacRae), who has a distinguished record as an educationalist, asked why the requirement with respect to a declaration of residence is proposed to be deleted in the draft bill. I think that the explanation is to be found in the fact that essentially the bill calls for the maintenance of the requirement of a year's residence but stipulates that the person applying for a loan, who is not a citizen, must be a landed immigrant. It is my understanding that to become a landed immigrant a person must declare he has the intention to reside permanently in Canada. Therefore, it would seem to me that achieving the status of landed immigrant would be a more definite indication than the signing of a simple declaration that the person wishes to remain in our country as a permanent resident and make his life here.
The basic purpose of this provision is to make clear that those who come here with student visas are not intended to be covered by the Canada Student Loans Act. The reason for this is that by definition a person with a student visa is someone who has demonstrated he has the financial resources available to him to pursue the course of studies he has in
November 13, 1969

Canada Student Loans Act mind in this country. So, I think the point which concerned the hon. member is covered by requiring that someone who is not a citizen not only must reside here for a year but must become a landed immigrant in order to become eligible for a student loan.
The hon. member also asked for some explanation of the payments made to the province of Quebec, and of how they are made. He seemed rather concerned when I indicated, I guess by a shaking of the head, that it was a transfer not by way of fiscal equivalent but a real payment.
The details of the formula can be found in section 12 of the Act. It is a rather complicated formula and I will not take the time of the House to read it, but to use the words of the annual report it may be summarized as follows: The alternative payment made to a province which does not participate is based upon two factors, the actual payments by the minister to lenders for interest and other charges, and the population aged 18-24 in a non-participating province relative to the size of the same age group in participating provinces.
This formula permits determination of the amounts,that have been paid over the years to the province of Quebec. The total paid to the province of Quebec since the inception of the plan in 1964 is in the amount of some $7,334,000, and the payment in the year 196869, which is part of this total, was in the amount of some $2,900,000. We should recall that the federal government itself does not provide the moneys for the loans. As hon. members know the moneys are provided by the banks and certain credit unions. The federal government pays the interest on the loans made to students from the participating provinces during the period of their postsecondary studies and for six months thereafter.
Various members have commented upon the criteria for determining eligibility for loans, for example, the hon. member for York-Sunbury, the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) and the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Thomson). Some, like the hon. member for York-Sunbury, referred to the test to determine eligibility for loans in a way that was somewhat more sympathetic than other hon. members, including some in his own party. I do not quarrel with that because that is part of the process of debate in our parliamentary system. However, I would like to point out that the criteria for eligibility for loans are

not set forth in the Act itself or in any regulations made under the act by the federal government.
Basically, the Act says in effect that loans can be made only where a student presents a certificate of eligibility which is issued by an appropriate provincial authority, and to get such a certificate he has to demonstrate to that authority that he has attained a satisfactory scholastic standard and that he is in need of a student loan. As I have said, the criteria for need are not defined in the Act itself or in the regulations made under it, but instead in a set of criteria which reflect basically the provincial consensus on these matters. To reply to a very interesting point raised by the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley, this means that the act itself, so far as I am aware, does not define what would constitute an independent student, and therefore a change in any definition of such a student would not have to be carried out through amendment in the act itself but instead in the administrative criteria which have been worked out by the provinces.
Decisions on eligibility for loans and on amounts of loans are not made by any agency of the federal government but instead by provincial authorities who apply these criteria. Therefore hon. members who have raised problems that have been brought to their attention by students whose applications have been turned down, or who have received loans in amounts they do not consider satisfactory, should make attempts to see that the appeal procedure which is provided for in these criteria is used. This will enable those not satisfied with the decisions of the provincial authorities to have these decisions reviewed. I again stress that there is an appeal procedure set forth or called for in these criteria which have been developed through provincial consultation.
The hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. MacRae) also expressed the fear that many millions of dollars which have been paid out under student loans would prove uncollectable. However, I think the experience to date should provide some reassurance. If one looks at the annual report one can see that a number of students have already begun repaying loans. About 93 per cent were meeting their obligation on a regular basis. About 3.5 per cent encountered difficulties in meeting regular payments due to a variety of circumstances such as illness, or lack of steady employment, only about 3.5 per cent of those
November 13, 1969

now responsible for their repayment obligation seem to have tried to avoid their responsibility in some way. I think this speaks quite highly of the integrity and common-sense and of the soundness of the general approach by our young people who have taken advantage of the student loan program. In my opinion, it augurs well for the attitude of students in future who have not yet come to the stage of repaying their loans.
The hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Hales) stated that he felt the chartered banks should be called upon to make sure that those students-and I am saying again, Mr. Speaker, that the percentage so far is very small- who have not been meeting their obligations are required to do so. He asked whether there was some procedure followed by the federal government to make sure that the banks were doing all they could in this regard. I am happy to inform him that there is in fact an established procedure, which has been worked out between the guaranteed loans administration of the Department of Finance and the lending institution, whereby a series of steps have to be completed by the lender before it can submit a claim for payment by the federal government. I am not going to discuss these steps in detail, but they begin with the bank sending a letter and can culminate with court action and judgment taken by the bank against the defaulting borrower. Should one or more of these steps be omitted, a responsible officer of the bank must explain why to the government. In all cases where a claim for payment is submitted to the government, the bank officer must sign a statement to the effect that the loan is uncollectable at the present time.
I should point out, Mr. Speaker, that while the government does pay interest on student loans until the end of the sixth month after the month when the borrower ceases to be a full-time student, should a loan be defaulted, the government pays to the bank the outstanding principal amount but only any past due interest. This total amount, however, becomes a debt due the Crown and follow-up procedures are begun to attempt to recover these funds from the borrower. The federal government does not pay interest indefinitely to the banks on past due loans which they are not attempting to collect. I know the hon. member for Wellington (Mr. Hales), as chairman of the Public Accounts Committee, will be interested in having this reassurance.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) made some
Canada Student Loans Act very interesting comments on the social desirability of the student loan program and also made some reference to the Liberal program of 1963. As I recall, in so far as that program covered this area, it had basically three parts: One, a system of youth allowances; second, creation of a student loan program, and third, a scholarship or bursary program. I think it is well to recall that two of these three programs have been implemented. The youth allowance program is in operation as the student loan program and of course we also have had for several years a program under which the federal government has been paying half the operating costs of postsecondary education. This program is costing the federal government hundreds of millions of dollars. Comments have been made about the social desirability of student loan programs and how they should fit into the general spectrum of student aid.
I might say that I, personally, do not consider that student loan programs will turn out to be the final word on the subject of efforts by governments-and I use the word in the plural-to make certain that all who are capable and desirous of post-secondary education have access to it. Canadians generally have been increasingly willing to support, as a desirable and necessary goal, steps to insure that everyone is able to get all the education desired, irrespective of personal financial resources. However, to achieve this goal calls for effort by more than one level of government. Since under our present constitution education is essentially a provincial matter, this means that any federal activity in this field must take into account this fact of Canadian life. Aside from what the present Canadian constitution provides in this area the provinces appear to have strong views as to the extent that the federal government should attempt to operate in what presently appears to be essentially a field of provincial jurisdiction. It seems to me that our movements toward this goal have to be made within this particular context. In saying this, one should not forget that the Canada student loan program has helped many students get post-secondary education who probably would not have otherwise had the resources to do so. I think this is demonstrated by the facts of the operation of the program. In 1964-65,
42,000	students received loans under the program. In the past year, this number increased to 107,000.
We could of course talk at length, Mr. Speaker, about improvements that could possibly be made to this program but I think we
November 13, 1969

Canada Student Loans Act should not forget that what has been done represents a real allocation of resources by the federal government to student aid. If this plan were not in existence, these resources might possibly have gone into other areas of priority. The federal government has not simply guaranteed payment of loans. Since the beginning of the plan in 1964, a total of some $23 million has been paid for interest, the relatively small amount of claims and alternative payments to Quebec. And certainly these amounts for interest and so on can be expected to increase in future years.
A number of hon. members, Mr. Speaker, have made suggestions for changes in the plan, for addition of different categories of students or changes in the maximum amounts that may be borrowed. For example, several hon. members called for the inclusion of parttime students in the plan. It is true that at the moment the plan only provides for loans to full-time students, but it should not be forgotten that its main purpose is to assist students to obtain education through full-time study so that the education need not be dragged on over several years. In many cases, part-time students hold employment which would assist in paying costs. At the time the plan was originally presented and adopted by Parliament the intention was that it cover full-time students only.
It should be kept in mind when looking at the question of broadening the plan or including other categories or changing the general approach, that when it was introduced in 1964 it was as a broad general measure in the student aid field. It was not intended to meet all the needs of all students seeking postsecondary education but was designed to supplement resources available to students from their own efforts and their families as well as other private or provincial student aid funds. As a reflection of this fact, the maximum individual loan amount of $1,000 did not, even in the first loan year, meet the entire average cost of a student's attendance at a post-secondary institution. As hon. members have pointed out, it is true that costs have increased since that time and $1,000 will now finance a relatively smaller portion of the total costs involved. One should not forget, however, that in 1964-65 the Canada student loans plan was the only major government measure in the student aid field. Since then there has been a dramatic increase in the volume of student aid made available by provincial governments which has helped offset rising costs.

The demand by most students, educationalists and others has been for increased grant aid rather than loans in order to minimize the loan burden on students. Programs of student aid in several provinces have been moving in this direction. One should keep this in mind when calling for an increase in the maximum amount of loans, annually or in total. I think at least one hon. member called for such an increase. However, other hon. members pointed out the problem that could be created if students should graduate with a heavy burden of debt. The maximum loan amount that could be obtained by a student for his postsecondary education under the plan was fixed originally with a view to taking into account the problem that could be created by imposing on the student an undue burden of debt after he graduates.
[DOT] (3:10 p.m.)
It is my understanding that the provinces are in the process of reviewing, together with the council of ministers of education, the whole field of student aid. The federal government has said that, if invited by them, it would be pleased to take part in this review. Therefore, in spite of the very interesting arguments made by various hon. members with regard to changing in some significant way the structure of the Canada student loans plan, it would not seem appropriate, in view of this ongoing review, that consideration should be given to making basic changes in the program until this review has been completed.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte), and the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquarrie) have raised the question of maximum amounts under the Canada Student Loans Act.
I want to say that the purpose of the bill is to guarantee sufficient money to meet loan requirements and this is why we are asking the House to approve the increased loan provision.
According to my information, the federal government has always taken the necessary steps to make sure that there is enough money to meet student loan requirements throughout Canada. It is the main reason why the government is introducing this bill now.
As far as I know no student has ever been refused a loan because provincial allocations were insufficient.
November 13, 1969
These allocations have always been adjusted so as to meet needs of students everywhere in Canada.

Dealing with another point raised by the hon. member for Hillsborough (Mr. Macquar-rie), I seem to recall him making references to age limits in the Canada Student Loans Act. There is, I should like to assure him, no age limit in the act as far as eligibility for loans is concerned. Perhaps he noted the reference in my remarks to the 18 to 24 years age group. This reference was made solely to help to describe the formula which was used for determining the division of the total amounts permissible in the participating provinces.
The hon. member for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) has brought to the attention of the House the problem of people who have encountered difficulty in meeting repayment terms for various reasons. She mentioned a case where one person was not able to make payments because he was not able to find permanent employment. I should like to assure her and this House that such situations are in fact provided for by the regulations. There exists in the regulations a considerable degree of flexibility in setting the terms of repayment to fit the ability of the borrower to repay or for changing them where the borrower's financial circumstances are, for one reason or another, upset. In addition, there is considerable consultation between the guaranteed loans administration and the lending institutions where genuine cases of hardship are encountered. The important thing for the borrower falling into this sort of difficulty to remember is that he should consult with the bank as soon as possible. I am informed that almost in all cases where complications arise for borrowers in this category, they do so because they have failed to advise the lender of their circumstances. So, the existing regulations do appear to provide sufficient flexibility to take care of the types of cases the hon. member has raised. Therefore, it would not appear necessary to call for an amendment to the act itself to deal with such problems.
To conclude, Mr. Speaker, may I say by way of conclusion, to hon, members that I would be very happy to receive any questions or complaints they may have brought to their attention from time to time about the operation of the Canada student loans plan.
Small Businesses Loans Act
If the matters in question happen to fall within that aspect of the plan which is directly under federal administration, that is matters having to do chiefly with the relationship between the government and the banks which make the loans, I would be happy to have them looked into and, if possible, dealt with in a satisfactory way. If they deal with aspects that come under provincial administration, including aspects dealing with questions of eligibility which I have outlined, I would be very happy to inform hon. members as to the steps they should take to have them reviewed by provincial authorities; or, if they prefer, I would be happy to make sure myself that these matters are looked into by provincial authorities. I hope hon. members will feel free to avail themselves of my willingness to assist them in dealing with problems of this type.
I will conclude, therefore, by saying that we have certainly had a very good discussion during this second reading stage. I look forward to going into other aspects which I have not had the opportunity to deal with at this point when the bill is before the committee. I hope it will be agreed that, on the basis of my own initial presentation, and the discussion that has followed, this bill deserves the support of this House on second reading.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CATEGORIES OF LENDERS
speechtext:
that Bill C-9, to amend the Small Businesses Loans Act, be read the

November 13, 1969

Small Businesses Loans Act second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in this bill are proposed a number of amendments to the Small Businesses Loans Act. The small businesses loans program is one of a group of three commercially oriented guaranteed loans programs under federal government auspices. They are designed to make available federally guaranteed term credit from private financial institutions to small businessmen, farmers and fishermen, to enable them to undertake a wide variety of expansion and improvement projects. The companion acts, therefore, to the Small Businesses Loans Act are the Farm Improvement Loans Act and the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act.
The Small Businesses Loans Act, first passed in 1960, provided for an initial three-year lending period. The act has subsequently been amended from time to time to provide for additional lending periods. Under the legislation, businessmen engaged in a number of fields of activity can obtain loans of up to $25,000 to finance a large number of business improvement projects. A small business is defined in the Act as one which has estimated gross revenues of less than $500,000 in the year in which it applies for the loan and which is engaged in one of the following forms of business activity: manufacturing, retail trade, wholesale trade, provision of services, construction, transportation and communication.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
Borrowers may use the proceeds of loans to finance the purchase of fixed or movable assets or equipment or for the purchase, construction or improvement of business premises. Small business loans must generally be secured by a first charge on machinery or equipment purchased or a mortgage on business premises. In addition, the borrower must sign a promissory note and the bank may, if it considers it advisable, require further securities to be given in order to secure a loan. Loans may be repaid over a period of up to 10 years. The act does not place the banks under any obligation to make such loans. In fact, it is a requirement of the legislation that they exercise the same care in the making of small business loans as they do in the general conduct of their business.
Lending under the Small Businesses Loans Act has proved to be relatively stable, ranging between $20 million and $26 million in


each year since the beginning of the program, with the exception of 1967 when the volume of loans declined to $11 million. From the time this program was started until November, 1968, the maximum rate of interest which banks could charge on loans made under the program was established under the regulations at 5i per cent.
For some time prior to 1968, however, the general level of interest rates had been moving steadily upward and during 1968 this movement accelerated. The result of this was to make the 5J per cent maximum rate unrealistic in relation to other avenues of investment which were open to lenders. In November of 1968 an order-in-council was made which changed the basis on which the maximum rate for small business loans was determined. This rate is now established twice annually, April 1 and October 1, and is based on the average of certain government of Canada bond yields over the preceding six months, plus a margin of 1 per cent. For the current period, October 1 of this first to March 31 next, this maximum rate is 8J per cent. Since the interest rate procedure was implemented, lending has returned to levels closer to the levels of past years.
I now wish to outline the amendments to the Small Businesses Loans Act proposed in Bill C-9. These amendments parallel changes which have been made to the Farm Improvement Loans Act and the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act in the past year or so. If the present amendments are adopted by Parliament, these three programs will operate on a consistent and comparable basis. The amendments will enable trust companies, insurance companies, mortgage loan companies as well as credit unions, Caisses Populaires and other co-operative credit societies to apply to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) for designation as eligible lenders under the Small Businesses Loans Act. This will parallel changes made in other guaranteed loans legislation and considerably broaden the types of financial institutions from which small businessmen may seek financing under this act.
The current lending period would, in the absence of amendment, expire on December 31 of this year. Among the amendments being proposed, therefore, is one which will add an additional 18 month period which will expire on June 30, 1971. This will result in the lending period under the Small Businesses Loans Act ending at the same time as the current lending periods under both the Farm Improvement Loans Act and the Fisheries
November 13, 1969

Improvement Loans Act. This will enable the government to review these three very similar programs as a group when they next come up for renewal. Possible changes in each can then readily be assessed in light of the implications which it holds for the others.
Under the Small Businesses Loans Act there is a two-fold limitation of the extent of the liability of the Minister of Finance for loans made. The first of these relates to the aggregate value of loans made by all lending institutions in a lending period. For the current lending period this over-all maximum was established at $300 million. During the new lending period established by these amendments, this amount is to be set at $100 million in respect of loans made by all chartered banks and $50 million in respect of loans made by all other eligible lenders.
The second part of the minister's liability deals with its extent to an individual lender. Currently, the liability is limited to an amount equal to 10 per cent of the gross value of loans made by any one lender. Since only the chartered banks had been eligible lenders in the past and since each had a sizeable amount of loans under the act, this in practice amounted to a 100 per cent guarantee as 10 per cent of the aggregate loans made by each was more than enough to pay out in full balances owing to banks on defaulted loans.
This provision could, however, expose a lender with only a few loans to the risk that if there was to be default on even one or two of them, there would be insufficient guarantee to cover the entire amount of the loss to the lender. In order to minimize this possibility, the liability of the minister to an individual lender will now be set at an amount equal to 90 per cent of the aggregate value of the first $125,000, 50 per cent of the amount between $125,000 and $250,000, and 10 per cent of the amount in excess of $250,000 of loans made by that lender. It is hoped that this revision will encourage the making of small business loans even at the low volume of lending by the individual classes of lenders who will be eligible to do so under the proposed amendments.
In conclusion, I wish to say it is the government's hope that these amendments will be of help to the small businessmen in Canada who constitute an important element of our economy. While lending under this program has never approached the volume under the Farm Improvement Loans Act, it has none the less been a useful source of term financing for the
Small Business Loans Act small businessmen. Since its inception some
20,000	small businesses have obtained financing of almost $190 million under this program. The proposals in Bill C-9 will ensure that this kind of credit facility will continue to be available to assist small businessmen in Canada.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF CATEGORIES OF LENDERS
speechtext:
On reading Bill C-9, an act to amend the Small Businesses Loans Act, one finds that section 1(a) extends the definition of a bank within the meaning of the Act to credit unions, caisse populaire, trust companies, loan companies and insurance companies. When the Bank Act was revised in 1966, the government refused amendments defining the business of banking in such a way as to bring credit unions and institutions of this type, carrying on all the functions of banking, under the control of the Bank Act. Yet, in this bill the government is deliberately amending an Act so as to define these institutions as banks. I have no quarrel with this, but it does give me the feeling there is some inconsistency in planning by the government.
The thought occurs to me, why should trust companies be included in this bill? I wonder whether they have actually sought the change to allow them to engage in this business or if this is merely wishful thinking on the part of the government. With a measure of this kind, it is necessary to examine how effective it has been and how many people are making use of these small business loans. I now wish to refer to the annual report of the Small Businesses Loans Act. I find that in the period 1961 to 1965, the total of the loans remained constant at $26 million per year. In the period 1966-1967, this amount decreased to $20 million. In 1968, the figure decreased to $11 million, or slightly more. I think we can draw a parallel to this, to some extent. If hon. members will look at the report on the operation of the Farm Improvement Loans Act they will find there was a gradual build-up to a point at which something between $200 millions and $212 million was being lent in the years from 1965 to 1967. Then, in 1968 it dropped to $40 million, or a little more, which represents a far greater decline than is evident even in small business loans under the legislation we are considering.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
It is interesting to compare these figures with those of the Industrial Development Bank operating in an area where the interest rate has been allowed to rise. We note at once
782	COMMONS
Small Business Loans Act the absence of a similar decline in the amount of money lent. The current I.D.B. rate of interest is something like 10 per cent on amounts less than $50,000, whereas the rate for the small business loans would be 8J per cent. Knowing the demand which exists for credit at the present time it is obvious there must be definite reasons for the sharp decline in the amount of money lent under the Act now before us.
Three reasons come to my mind. First, the Act could be too restrictive-it might not seem to be, but possibly it could be interpreted by the banks in terms which are too restrictive. It may be we should broaden the scope of this Act so as to cover more types of business, or more lines of credit. We should certainly encourage the use of loans of this type. I am sure hon. members looking back to their ridings, would agree it is much better to have 50 businesses employing 20 people each than to have one business employing 1,000.
Another reason, and one which in my view can be advanced with a greater degree of certainty, follows from the fact that no loan can exceed $25,000. While this may have been realistic back in 1961, it is not even in the ball park today. I do not intend to discuss the changes in the price structure and in the cost of living index since 1961, because we are all familiar with this situation, but I will say that a maximum figure of $40,000 or $50,000 would be far more in line with the credit requirements of business today. The I.D.B. figures certainly indicate that loans in the higher category are more generally required.
The third reason which occurs to me, and I believe it is probably the main reason, is the reluctance of the banks to lend money under this Act. This situation might be partially corrected by the amendment which would increase the percentage of the guarantee for banks whose aggregate amount on loan under the Act did not exceed $250,000. Nevertheless,
I cannot but feel there is a reluctance on the part of the financial institutions to lend money at the current rate of 8i per cent when it is possible for them to do considerably better.
We are all aware that the banks have an obligation to this country and to its citizens. When Parliament granted them a charter to service the money market and create credit they accepted this obligation. I submit, from our experience of the operation of this Small Businesses Loans Act and of the Farm Improvement Loans Act, that they are not

DEBATES	November 13, 1969
living up to their obligation. We can see the demand for loans generally is increasing. But instead of fulfilling their obligations under their charters, our banks are simply going after bigger profits. They are going after the dollar, that is all it boils down to, and they are not concerned with small business; they are not concerned with the people. They would much prefer to put their money where there is no risk and where interest rates are higher than to lend it under this small loans legislation. It is time the minister put his finger on the banks and told them: Live up to your obligations to the citizens of this country or maybe we should revoke your charter.
The banks have a responsibility and it is the duty of the government to see they live up to the terms of their charters. If we allow the present situation to continue we could eventually find the banks lending all their money to the large corporations. General Motors, for example, could use far more capital than is needed for all the small business and farm improvement loans put together. I believe the banks are tending to look at the situation in this light. They are not conscious of any pressure on them to fulfil their obligations, and they are by-passing small borrowers. Look at the amounts set aside for guarantees as compared with the amount used under this Act-something like $100 million set aside for each year, and only $11 million used last year. We know the demand is there, so we can only conclude that a great deal must be wrong in this area.
Last week the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) put his finger on the small businesses of this nation. His white paper on taxation said, in effect, to small businessmen, the middle class of this country: Live up to your obligation to the poor. But he is not doing anything to affect the real wealth of this country. The tax rates to be imposed on certain income levels will be dropping from 80 per cent to 50 per cent. If the minister is willing to put his finger on small businesses and private entrepreneurs, I say he should be willing to put his finger on the banks and tell them to live up to their responsibilities, too.
When we look at the financial statements of the banks we find they are not suffering any hardship. I have a statement here from the Royal Bank of Canada from which I note that in the last three years, from 1966 to 1968, net profits rose from $27 million to $35J million. There is certainly no reason for the banks to complain about their profit margin. They should be forced, if necessary, to go out into
November 13, 1969

the market and extend credit where it is needed.
I do not believe one can consider this bill adequately without at the same time taking into account the ramifications of the white paper on tax reform, if and when they are implemented-and there is every indication from the government that they will be. Most of the small businesses that will obtain loans under Bill C-9 are what the white paper describes as closely held corporations, and for taxation purposes will be taxed at rates similar to those applied to unincorporated businesses. When a small businessman takes a loan under this Act-the same can be said of farmers taking farm improvement loans-a contract is entered into for a period of time. I believe the time limit on small business loans is up to ten years. In many cases, these loans will extend into the period when the proposed plans in the government's white paper on taxation come into effect.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
Present borrowers are contracting to repay their loans in a given period knowing that the tax rate under our present corporate structure is 21 cents on the dollar on amounts under $35,000, the sort of loans we are mostly concerned with here. What happens to these businesses when the government changes the rules in the middle of the ball game? The borrower who has contracted to repay his loan at the current taxation rate is suddenly put into the position of being called upon to pay 130 per cent of his present rate of taxation. By way of additional burden, he may also be paying 50 per cent tax on paper profits supposedly accrued from a misplaced valuation date.
In short, Mr. Speaker, I say that these amendments will do absolutely nothing for the small businessman unless the finance minister puts his finger in present banking policy. May I also say there is little benefit bestowed by legislation that we hope will encourage small businesses and private entrepreneurs when there is already on the drafting board a systematic program that will lead to the eventual destruction of such private enterprises.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to draw to the attention of the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Gray) that this time both the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Downey) and the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley
Small Business Loans Act are participating in the debate, and since it is reasonable to suggest that he may become confused perhaps he should not quote us directly.
First of all, may I put a direct question to the minister in the hope that he will reply to it when he closes the debate. My question concerns how the Department of Finance intends to supervise and guarantee loans that are made by authorized corporations. The reason I raise this question is that an insurance company, authorized under provincial legislation in Ontario, recently went bankrupt with particularly messy results. In this case many investors lost their money. I would not want to see any federal taxation money going down a similar type of drain, so perhaps the minister will explain how he intends to supervise companies who lend money under a federal guarantee in accordance with the terms of the act.
As we all know, Mr. Speaker, there has been a trend in recent years for small businesses to be swallowed up by the large corporations. Sometimes small businesses are bought up; on other occasions direct competition has been successful in forcing the small businessman to the wall. I hope this bill will provide him with some relief in this regard. Certainly, the small businessman needs capital, and in a time of inflation and tight money it is extremely difficult to find.
I suggest this bill can be likened to a piece of string. Although you can give the string some leeway, and let it out a little, you cannot exert pressure on it. Similarly, you cannot persuade a small businessman to borrow money unless he wishes to do so. Neither can you force a bank to lend him that money. I wonder whether the minister would consider this legislation in that light, because perhaps a little leeway on the string might be required as far as credit institutions are concerned.
The small businessman frequently finds himself in the awkward position of passing on increased costs to his customers. In times of continually rising interest rates, he finds himself in a more awkward position in this respect than do some of the larger firms. I think some consideration should be given to the fact that small businesses are less able to pay high interest rates than the big corporations.
I also wonder whether something could be done for the small businessman by way of training. Let me give an example of what I mean. Take the man who is an exceptionally
784	COMMONS
Small Business Loans Act able automobile mechanic. Soon, he is promoted to shop foreman, and then eventually, having saved money and perhaps borrowed some from his relatives, the bank, or the credit union under this particular legislation, he purchases the business and goes into business for himself. He is now in a completely different field; no longer is he repairing automobiles or tractors. From experience I have had with others, I feel it would be useful to establish some sort of business management training scheme. Although we have training schemes for mechanics that want to turn to some other trade, to my knowledge there is no adequate government-sponsored training offered in the field of business management.
As a farmer, I was once a member of a farm management club, and I am fully aware of what membership in that club did for me as a small businessman. I suggest the government should consider establishing, either by bringing pressure to bear on provincial governments or in co-operation with provincial governments, a management training scheme for small businessmen who are required to manage businesses. This is particularly necessary when a man leaves a trade and enters the field of business management. Whether these people are in the newspaper business, are workers in garages, tinsmiths or plumbers, most of them have moved up the ladder through their trade, and I think something of the kind I have outlined should be done for them. It is tragic when men who have saved money for 25 years and who have borrowed money to go into business lose all within five years, plus five years off their lives. I know people to whom this has happened, and all they really needed was a little more management skill.
There has also been quite an expansion of the franchising field recently. I think that this sort of business enterprise has considerable merit. In some cases it provides more efficiency, and it offers the individual an opportunity to participate at the local level. I think it is good to have franchising rather than having big companies run everything from the top. I am happy to see the expansion. It is not always the best thing, in so far as price competition is concerned, to have this difference in the positions of the two elements. Frequently, the local businessman finds he has to work long hours for little or nothing, making sacrifices to make ends meet, whereas the big company has arranged to be in a protected position. Perhaps we should have legislation which offers some protection to the man who

DEBATES	November 13, 1969
finds himself in competition with a big company. There are many in this position and the number is apt to increase. Perhaps the minister would consider legislation of this nature.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate on Bill C-9, because it has to do with industry and improvements to the small businesses loans program.
Some of these amendments will enable the caisses populaires to participate in this loans program.
Presently, I do not see how the problem could be solved this way.
Certainly we are facing a financial problem we will not solve by creating new debts, by granting new loans, by setting prohibitive interest rates.
As an example, I will take the Industrial Development Bank which is now making loans to industries at an 11 or 12 per cent interest rate. Is it by maintaining this practice, in the case of Caisses Populaires or other institutions lending under similar conditions, that we will solve the industrialization problem? The only thing we achieve this way is to encourage industry to incur further debts it cannot repay. In fact, its production costs will increase so much that it will be unable to distribute its production because the consumers will never have the necessary purchasing power to buy the surplus production.
November 13, 1969	COMMONS DEBATES	797
Several industries would not need capital at the present time nor would they have to pay prohibitive interest rates, if they could find a market to sell their products. We can finance production as much as we want to, but if we do not finance consumption, we will only aggravate the existing uneasiness.
But industry is compelled to finance consumption and buyers because the latter have no buying power. And industry is bound to do this for five, six or twelve months and to secure repayment bit by bit or to force the debtors to pay. That is one of the reasons why industry can no longer operate: it has to pile up stocks, to enlarge premises and to support consumers.
That explains why important reserves of capital are necessary to run an industry. When capital has to be borrowed at present interest rates which are exorbitant very little progress is possible in industry.
Here is how this will come out: we are going to help industry fill its warehouses and sell on credit even more. But one of these fine days, there will be all kinds of bankruptcies. Small business in particular will go bankrupt because they will be unable to sell their products and will have to pay too much interest to keep their inventories and their buyers.
There is the rub. Many small businesses could well do without such charges if they were able to sell out their products and get paid. That is one of the reasons why I wanted to rise and speak on this bill.
Our problem is of an economic nature. It is one of distribution, rather than one of production, because, at the present time, in 1969, our gross national product amounts to $72 billion. Canada has consumed $40 billion of it, and with $40 billion we want to purchase $72 billion's worth of goods. It is impossible. Consumers should pay $40 billion for products valued at $72 billion. This is where we should intervene. This is where adjustments should be made. This overproduction costs nothing to anyone. It is a surplus of the society at large, a surplus for all Canadians who are shareholders of their country, a surplus which should be distributed under the form of compensated discount in order to reduce prices and bring them in line with the purchasing power. This is what I wanted to say. There surely are solutions.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
At the present time, instead of trying to remedy the situation, we aggravate it. The more we apply the system, the more 21362-51
Small Business Loans Act unbalanced becomes our economy. What is needed is a balanced economy which we will arrive at by adjusting prices rather than setting them. This is where we should intervene.
Production represents $72 billion and consumption is equivalent to $40 billion. Production is equal to consumption. Consumers should pay $40 billion for that production. That is the point where prices should be adjusted. Otherwise, we will no longer succeed in balancing a productive, active, mechanized and technical economy, from which would issue an automated production requiring no employer.
We shall not settle the problem by granting loans. We are not against loans. We want the small industries to carry on. We very well know that the problem will remain the same and that the burden of the debt will simply increase.
The desired goal will only be reached through the implementation of a banking policy designed to provide the necessary funds both for the production of the goods that our human and material resources make physically possible, and for the proper distribution of all our national production or the equivalent.
If there is no money to make production possible in order to meet human and normal needs, and if it becomes plentiful when production and means of production are requisitioned to pay soldiers and to make deadly weapons, it is because the present monetary system is imposing decisions instead of proudly reflecting the facts resulting from the free action of free producers and free consumers. So this is why we should get to the heart of the problem and find appropriate solutions.
The first proposal is aimed at insuring maximum purchasing power by achieving a balance between consumer prices and the total amount of money available to purchasers.
If production is to achieve its end, which is consumption, it is necessary to establish a price adjustment machinery, instead of fixing prices. It is up to the producers themselves to determine their cost prices, for they know their production costs.
During the last financial year, the country's production has reached $72 billion and consumption $44 billion, in round figures. The $72 billion production has then cost the country $44 billion. The $28 billion must be supplied by another source, not by the buyers. The monetary system should see to that.
November 13, 1969

Small Business Loans Act
In other words, there should be a general compensated discount which would be the contrary of a sales tax and this compensated discount should be applied to all the retail prices for the duration of the financial year which is beginning. At the end of each financial year,, the general compensated discount should be calculated in the light of consumption and in relation to the production volume.
Thus we would come as close as possible to the ideal purchasing power. This operation would be called a compensated price or discount, because the money which the seller does not get from the purchaser owing to that discount, he would get later on from the national credit board. This compensation granted to the seller so that he may get his full cost price, safeguards all interests and benefits everyone through the easy flow of goods to meet the needs. Production is intended to be sold.
If industry is to be reorganized, it is impossible to do so simply with loans in the case of private industry. Here I distinguish between private industry and capital stock industry.
Private industry has to reimburse its capital, pay interest and pay its taxes, and the loans it raises result in bankruptcy for 99 per cent of the small companies.
So what is the use of creating such a situation, organizing industries in such a way that they cannot prosper. All our present efforts are useless. Share-capital industries, since they do not have to reimburse capital, can manage to scrape through, although many of them will be unable to make it.
So what we are heading for is socialism, centralization, an appalling slump, utter destruction of private enterprise. With the present tax pattern, no private industry, no merchant can manage to pay debts as well as provincial, municipal, school and other taxes.
In these conditions, it is impossible for a small industry to become prosperous and to make profits if it cannot dispose of its products. Even though we invest more in industry, we do not inject into it more purchasing power because our investments are used to pay for the machinery and the buildings. They are "dead" investments which hardly contribute to put money in circulation.
Nowadays, an industry which employs 10 people can be compared to one which employed 200 people 20 years ago, taking into consideration automation, science and progress.
I would have a lot more to say but I think that other hon. members wish to speak on this

matter. As for me, I consider that I have done my share.
I am sure that the increase in the amount of these loans will not improve the economic situation of industry.

Mr. Speaker, it would now appear appropriate for me to rise and finalize this debate on second reading by attempting to reply to at least some of the points raised by hon. members earlier in the day. The hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Downey) made a comment regarding the wording of the amendment which makes it possible for credit unions, caisses populaires, trust companies and other credit societies to take part in the small businesses loan program. I should stress that in spite of the form of the wording used, the act does not purport to make these institutions into banks for all purposes. The effect of the wording used is simply to enable the institutions in question to participate in this guaranteed loans program. I suggest there really is no conflict therefore with the policy of the government at the time the Bank Act was studied by Parliament. We must remember that as its name implies this is a guaranteed loans program under which the government guarantees that the institutions which make the loans shall not suffer loss. It would appear that the effect of having a more flexible interest rate formula has been to encourage banks to make more money available for loans of this type. This is implied by the most recent figures which are available.
Some hon. members have suggested that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) should take some kind of action to have the banks make even more money available for the purpose of this program. However, as far as I am aware the Bank Act does not give the Minister of Finance the type of authority under which he could order banks to participate in this or any of the other guaranteed loans program to any particular extent. However, the banks may be interested in noting the view expressed by hon. members in this debate, to the effect that they have not been living up to their responsibility to the community by making sufficient funds available for loan to small businesses.
November 13, 1969

Small Business Loans Act
Several hon. members have used this debate as a vehicle through which to express their views regarding some of the proposals in the government's white paper on tax reform. While these views are very interesting, I think the degree of concern expressed may well be proven excessive after hon. members have experience of the impact of the proposals on small businesses. I shall not attempt to debate these proposals at this point. I am sure there will be many opportunities to do so either before the standing committee or when the government presents a bill to the House following the report of the standing committee on the proposals.
I think it is worthwhile for hon. members and the public generally to very carefully study them before reaching definite conclusions about their possible effects. As I have said, it may be that the initial reactions to the proposals which were reflected in some speeches this afternoon may not have indicated exactly what the real impact of the proposals will be on small businessmen.
Several hon. members advanced interesting suggestions regarding changes in the small businesses loans program. Therefore I would like to point out that the basic effect of having the lending period under the program terminate at the same time as the two other government guaranteed loans programs will be that the government will make a thorough review of the effectiveness of the small businesses loans program together with its two companion guaranteed loans programs. I am sure it will be possible in the course of this review to give consideration to the suggestions which have been made.
[DOT] (8:30 p.m.)
Some hon. members have argued, in effect, that the proposals before us will not really do anything to help small businessmen. However, we should recognize that if this bill is not supported by the House it will not be possible to carry on a small businesses loans program at all once the current lending period ends. If this bill is passed it will mean that the program can continue for a further lending period. As the hon. member for Wellington-Grey (Mr. Howe) has pointed out, some 20,000 loans have been made under this program to date. This is an indication that it has been playing a useful role in helping small business to exist and, hopefully, to expand and thrive. I might add that the presentation of the amendments at this time is a demonstration that the government is .certainly not against small business.


The hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Thomson) asked me how the Department of Finance intends to supervise loans which, if this bill is adopted, would be made by trust companies and other institutions under provincial jurisdiction. The approach the department will be taking is that when an application is made by a provincially incorporated or provincially chartered institution for designation under the program, the application will be referred to the Superintendent of Insurance for his comments and consideration of the institution's financial soundness. Only after his report has been received would a decision be made as to whether the provincially incorporated institution in question should be designated for the purpose of the act. Once approval had been given, the appropriate branch of the Department of Finance would keep an eye on its work through a series of established practices with the aim of seeking to avoid the type of problem to which the hon. member referred.
Finally, I can say that the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation can give coverage to provincial institutions and I am informed that almost all the provincially chartered trust and loan companies are in fact under the supervision of that corporation. As I said earlier, I shall not attempt to comment on all the interesting suggestions which have been made; these matters can be dealt with in the course of the review of the program which the government intends to carry out, as well as in the discussions before the standing committee.

In addition, the bill does not force provincial institutions to participate automatically in the program. It is up to them to ask that

maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS, AIR CANADA PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in debating Bill C-7 we are adopting in essence, as the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Gray) has stated, what to many is a customary and standard procedure. The opportunity to discuss this bill in the House is timely in view of the confused state of railroading and transportation in Canada. It gives us the chance to examine the financial budget and expenditure both of Canadian National Railways and Air Canada.
I note at the very beginning of my remarks that money for these companies has already been appropriated for the year 1969 and most of the $201 million being appropriated by this bill has already been spent. I think it is poor


administration from the legislative point of view to examine a bill appropriating money that has already been spent. But this being the case, all we can do is to ask whether the money has been spent well. It is from this point of view that I propose to examine the bill. I want to determine whether the money has been spent wisely, and whether or not Air Canada and the CNR have met the obligation imposed upon them of satisfying the transportation needs of all Canadians.
Canada today finds herself involved in the great emotional question of whether she can survive as a nation. Is Canada a viable entity? What part does transportation play in holding the country together? To my mind, transportation without doubt is still the key to the economic survival of Canada, particularly in that part of Canada in the proximity of the 49th parallel. I see in Canada today great concern and unhappiness with our transportation complex. The costing system that has been approved by the Canadian Transport Commission is being appealed to the Supreme Court. Passenger traffic is in a state of complete chaos and so is air passenger traffic, with which I will deal later in my remarks. The three major components of our transportation industry-freight and passenger rail traffic and air traffic-are in confusion. For the moment I exclude trucking and pipelines.
1 have with me this evening a poem that was written some time ago by a well known resident of Alberta. I think it correctly spells out the difficulty in which we find ourselves in Canada today. If the House will bide with me for a moment or two I should like to read this poem, because I think it puts rather clearly before Canadians the picture of our railroads today. The poem was written by a person called "Ferg" James and is called "Farewell to the Old Iron Horse". It reads as follows:
They opened up a continent,
They brought the settlers in They colonized a nation,
With every kith and kin.
They did a yeoman service,
Their laurels they have won,
Now the giants of the frontier Have made their final run.
We miss their belching smokestacks,
And their whistle's moan and scream We miss the throbbing pistons,
And the hissing clouds of steam.
But their days were surely numbered,
They have vanished one by one,
And the grand old railroad steamers Have made their final run.
November 13, 1969

The water tanks stand empty,
Along the right of way The round house is foresaken,
Where the monsters used to stay.
The coal docks are a memory,
Their days of service done,
Since the big steam locomotives Have made their final run.
A sleek new shining diesel,
Came down the line today
And it makes you kind of wonder
Are these units here to stay?
With progress pressing onward,
And their era just begun As history keeps repeating Will they make their final run?
As we gaze into the future,
Of a hundred years or more
What scientific marvels
This old world may have in store.
A weird fantastic monster,
Getting power from the sun With ten million pounds of payload May be on their daily run.
I feel that that poem spells out the problems facing Canada today in the railroading and transportation field. If Canada were a small, compact country, transportation might not be a problem; but Canada is a great country stretching from the Atlantic to the Pacific and, as I said at the beginning of my remarks, transportation is the key to our economic survival. If Canada is to maintain a sound and viable economy, we must pay great attention to our transportation problems. If we take transportation for granted and allow our railroad companies to become conglomerates, paying no heed to the obligations they undertook in return for certain privileges granted to them when we started to build this country, we as legislators are failing in our duty.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
We see a host of expenditures here and, as I mentioned, the money has already been spent. Let us examine how it was spent so we may know whether it was spent wisely. Is the CNR to remain a "next year" railroad? Will we forever have to examine deficits of $29 million in 1968 and an estimated $25 million for 1969? This bill is a measure to cover that deficit. Will the railroad forever be coming back asking this government to pick up its deficits? During my speech I intended to ask the government to have this whole question referred to the transport committee. It should study costing, the question of branch line abandonment and freight rates, all of which are tied together. It should decide whether we need passenger service, and what is our air policy. All these things should be subject to a
DEBATES	803
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada comprehensive study by the transport committee.
It may well be suggested that the committee studied these matters a number of years ago. I know that it studied them, but if Canada is to remain economically solvent we must be on guard in respect of expenditures by our transportation systems. We must decide whether they are directed in the right way or whether they will make the CNR a "next year" railroad and Air Canada a "next year" air line.
What is our air policy? This question has been puzzling many people recently. We notice in this legislation a number of expenditures. Last year $79 million was spent by the CNR for passenger travel alone. In its application before the Canadian Transport Commission the CNR claimed it lost $11,600,000. How great a role has the Canadian Transport Commission played in respect of transportation in the last two years? One cannot say it has played a magnificent role, because it has not changed things. It has adopted a costing formula which has not satisfied the railways; they are appealing it to the Supreme Court. In other words, the Supreme Court must analyse the situation on the basis of research carried out by somebody; it must decide whether the railroad's costing system is better than the system proposed by the Transport Commission.
The Canadian transportation bill which this House passed a few years ago provides in principle that if a loss can be proved, the government will grant up to 80 per cent of that loss. If one is a shrewd businessman, as I know the CPR and CNR managers are, it is good business to appeal to the Canadian Transport Commission in an attempt to prove a gigantic loss. I have questioned this principle and I will continue to question it in my remarks tonight.
Let me re-emphasize the importance of this whole question being referred to the transport committee. I point out that the whole costing procedure is in question today. We must decide whether passenger train service is necessary and whether this was spelled out in the old Act of Parliament of 1881 which established the CPR. I have it before me and could read it. I may do so before I am through.
Is passenger service still necessary, and should the government pay 80 per cent of these fictitious losses which the railways present to the commission? We must also consider the whole question of our air policy. This
November 13, 1969
804	COMMONS
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada question was considered at a recent meeting in Ottawa of the Air Transport Association of Canada. At that meeting the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson)-that very amiable fellow-tried his best to spread oil on troubled waters. What has taken place? Let me quote from the Globe and Mail of November 6 of this year. This is a report of what took place at that meeting of the Air Transport Association attended by people involved in all aspects of air traffic in Canada, including regional carriers and I suppose Canadian Pacific. The article states:
The Air Transport Association of Canada in an unprecedented action yesterday moved a vote of no confidence in the air transport committee of the Canadian Transport Commission.
The Air Transport Committee is a body set up by this Parliament, yet the Transport Association says it has no confidence whatsoever in that body. We as members of parliament ought to be the watch-dogs of Canadian legislation. We should immediately have brought the members of the Air Transport Committee before the transportation committee of this House so that we as elected representatives could properly decide whether what is said in the article in the Globe and Mail is accurate. It suggests that directives have been made which cannot be carried out and are incapable of enforcement. Let me read further from this article:
The membership was told at that meeting the transport committee's general orders were considered unenforceable by the Transport Commission because of a Supreme Court of Canada decision last year that ruled that the Air Transport Committee did not have the power under the Aeronautics Act to issue orders.
Even the transport committee is making no attempt to enforce these directives. I spoke to the minister privately about this matter and suggested this was a deplorable situation in one of the fastest means of transportation in the country. He said he had been made aware of the situation and thought he had it covered. Where has he been? Where has the government been? I quote from the 1968 34th Annual Report of the Air Transport Association of Canada. This is what the chairman said over a year ago:
I would be remiss if I did not record the disappointment and frustration of this industry resulting from the confusion existing regarding government policy. Not only has there been no implementation of previously enunciated policy governing the mainline and regional carriers, but no extension of policy governing other segments of the industry has been developed. Virtually all Canadian air carriers are suffering under a tremendous handicap


in the development of plans, acquisition of new aircraft, and the continued operation of their companies on a profitable basis as action is delayed in providing effective air policy.
One could go on and read the whole 1968 annual report, but that is what was said in 1968 about the Air Transport Committee. I read from the Globe and Mail and what it said about this matter in 1969. One could also read from the 1967 and 1966 annual reports. Air passenger traffic and air freight have increased very rapidly in the last three or four years, but the air transport aspect of the Canadian Transport Commission has not kept up to date. The evidence of this is there for anyone to see. The bill now before us provides for another $165 million. We note that Air Canada is attempting to lower fares from Canada to Europe. If this is justified, where is all the money going? Certainly the people in the air transportation business do not know the answer to that question. They suggest that we do not have an air policy and that the policy we used to have is not enforced. Surely we should do better than this as elected representatives of the people of our great country.
Let us take a brief look at the passenger situation. As I mentioned, this bill covers the budget for 1968-69. The CNR has budgeted $79 million for passenger services in 1969. In 1968 it budgeted $81 million for passenger service. That is a lot of money. How does this compare with the situation in the CPR? Both the CNR and the CPR have submitted a long list of applications in respect of passenger services. They have asked the Board of Transport Commissioners to allow them to abandon these services, or if not to pay them the losses they incur. As I mentioned before, they have tremendously increased these losses. It is provided in the act under which they operate that if they can prove then-losses the government may grant them a subsidy in the amount of 80 per cent of those losses. The theory is that if they suffer the other 20 per cent of the loss it will help to keep them competitive and desirous of providing additional services. Is that really the case? We have an act which encourages the railways to go out of business. How does it do that? The railways must lose money on then-passenger services because then they can collect a subsidy. If they get a subsidy, then that is their bread and butter.
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)

speechtext:
Yes, 80 per cent is a lot of bread. As I have said before,, I believe the railways deliberately downgrade their services. We heard evidence before the committee to suggest this is the case, that is, that they do it deliberately in order to create a deficit so that they can ask for a subsidy. This is a deplorable situation. This is what the Transport Act suggests they do. When the Transport Act was passed by this House it said in effect that $110 million worth of subsidies would be cut out, but if the railways could prove they were losing business on any particular line they could come back to Parliament and would be granted 80 per cent of that loss. Since the end of centennial year, the year in which passenger services were profitable, the railways have attempted to prove that they are losing money on all their major passenger lines.
Let us study the two railways briefly. The CNR has four times as many passenger miles as the CPR. Revenue passenger miles are calculated by multiplying the number of paying passengers by the mileage they travel. The CNR has something like 2,246 million passenger miles; the CPR has something like 500 million passenger miles. It is obvious that the CNR carries over four times as many passengers over four times as much mileage. One would therefore think that if the passenger business was losing money, the losses of the CNR-according to their figures-would be four times greater than the losses of the CPR. The CPR has some very profitable lines and some short lines which are paying well. The CNR appears before the Canadian Transport Commission and files applications to discontinue some regional services on which they say they are losing $11.6 million. The CPR appears before the same board-and bear in mind it is travelling one quarter the distance-and says it is losing $30 million.
