speechtext: Shame.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS, AIR CANADA PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES
speechtext:
Now, from a quick look at these figures one will realize that the CPR is quickly building up a case for a huge subsidy. There is in the Financial Post dated November 15, 1969, a very interesting article on transportation and railways. I should like to read one paragraph:
CN President N. J. MacMillan told a House of Commons committee this spring that the two railroads and the Canadian Transport Commission have a study under way toward the development of a "coherent" national rail passenger system.
DEBATES	805
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada
With this vividly on the record it is obvious that we can hardly study CNR passenger traffic without studying CPR passenger traffic because the two, whether or not they admit it openly, as more or less in cahoots in an effort to create an atmosphere that they are losing huge amounts of money on their passenger services. I do not doubt that they may well be losing money on some lines. But should we as representatives from every region in Canada say that if they are losing money in one region they can discontinue the service? We are running a national, government-owned railway. Can we say that one region should not have passenger service and that all other regions should? I do not think we can do that.
We might ask ourselves what is the situation in respect of the CPR, what it was granted in 1881 and what obligation was placed upon it. When Mr. Sinclair appeared before the committee in 1966 he said that they accept their obligation, but in order to meet the obligation here must be an effective demand for the service. He said there is no point in living up to an obligation when people do not travel on the trains. I made the point earlier that the CPR have deliberately downgraded their services in order to create the fictitious figure of $30 million. What has really happened? What obligation is there upon the railways to create effective demand? If we are in business we must advertise in order to create an effective demand. So I say there is an obligation on the CPR and the CNR in this regard. I commend the CNR for its past action in respect of lowering fares and improving passenger services. From 1962 on a really good effort was made to encourage more passenger traffic on their trains. The CPR, however, has done exactly the opposite.
Back in 1881 when the government of the day was attempting to tie this great nation together, it started to build a railway line. It was given to the CPR. At that time the railroad that had been built was worth something in the order of $37 million. The CPR officials were told that they would be given a lot of right-of-way and a lot of money if they would complete the railroad. I shall not go into all the detail; it is to be found at page 1198 of the proceedings of the transport committee for the year 1966-67. What happened? The railway was completed by the CPR. The total amount of government money the CPR received, both direct and indirect, was $228 million. This was a lot of hay, particularly in those days when a dollar was a dollar.
806	COMMONS DEBATES	November 13, 1969
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
However, the inflated egos of the present government have inflated the value of money so that a dollar is not what it used to be. We are all aware of that. The point I am making is that the CPR continued to sell townsites all along the railway line. Prior to June, 1916, it sold land for townsites through the southern prairies and into British Columbia worth $123 million. This was land we gave the CPR. We encouraged the CPR to build and to develop Canada. I am not condemning that. It did a pretty good job. But now it comes along and says, "We have no further obligation. We sold the land for those townsites, but we have no obligation to continue passenger service for the people in those towns." I say they are reneging on the moral concept of the 1881 agreement, and I hope that the CTC, Parliament and the government will look into the whole question of the CPR.
I could go on and tell the House of the mineral wealth of the CPR and of the tremendous acreage granted to it. I do not need to tell you what the CPR has done with it. It now has Canadian Pacific Investments and Cominco, founded on the mineral wealth it was given under the original agreement. The CPR would like us to consider passenger service as a separate entity. I point out that railroads today are becoming conglomerates throughout the United States and Canada. It is good business sense that they should do so. I am not objecting to the CPR becoming a conglomerate, but I say it does not have the right to renege on the moral concept of the original agreement.
Can you imagine the whole southern half of the prairies being left without railway passenger service? It might be said that air service would fill the gap. But is there really air service for the little towns, with airplanes now getting larger to the point where the runways at some of the major prairie centres are not big enough to handle them? In this respect I think of the town from which the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Olson) comes, Medicine Hat, a thriving community, an old community in the province of Alberta; yet it is having a difficult time maintaining any kind of regional air transport service.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS, AIR CANADA PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES
speechtext: And it is a designated area.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS, AIR CANADA PROVISION FOR CAPITAL EXPENDITURES, GUARANTEEING OF SECURITIES
speechtext:
It is a designated area, and perhaps it should be. As airplanes become bigger and faster they will make fewer and fewer stops. The major concern in the future will be the location of airports. Even now

there is a fairly large body of opinion that Toronto and Montreal should share an airport located somewhere between them. But how will people get to such an airport? This was a project thought of a couple of years ago by a former minister of transport. Passenger service by the CNR and CPR is still necessary in many regions. Since 1962 the CNR has done a commendable job to attract passengers, but as I read present-day signs it is going to attempt to discontinue its drive toward that end and has now applied for a $11.6 million subsidy.
I say that the CNR should be something like the Post Office Department. It should not necessarily pay its way. It should provide service for Canadians in Newfoundland, Alberta, the Peace River country and in every part of our land. This is also the obligation that the CPR has to accept. It has a duty to provide a service because it was built under a special agreement; it was built with the money of Canadian people and it has a moral obliga'ion to them. As I say, I see signs that the CNR is discontinuing its drive to attract passengers. Just look at the great province of Newfoundland and what is happening to its rail service. We have to examine the whole problem, Mr. Speaker.
The Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) is sponsoring legislation to provide for standardization of safety in automobiles. Why are we concerned about automobile safety? It is because of the overloaded traffic on our highways? If the railroads modernized their services they can and will provide very effective commuter service and cut down on the number of automobiles on our highways. They can do so if, to use the common expression, they get with it.
What about the question of pollution? The Economic Council has dealt with it at length, particularly pollution in major population centres caused by automobiles. This is one of the major problems in areas of dense population. A fast, economical railroad commuter service would relieve the congestion on our highways and cut down the pollution caused in major centres throughout Canada such as Toronto, Montreal, Winnipeg and Vancouver. These cities are already examining the problem of pollution caused by carbon monoxide being emitted from automobiles.
Let us look at the cost of branch line services. Under this bill provision is made for the building of 140 miles of branch lines, at a cost of $19 million. Some $2J million are to be spent on building a railroad out to Robert's Bank. I suppose this is a good expenditure,
November 13, 1969	COMMONS
but it is a pretty narrow one in the sense that the Robert's Bank port will handle only coal while on occasion the port of Vancouver is congested with grain ships. We are spending $2J million to build a railroad to Robert's Bank on behalf of the Kaiser Corporation so that it may sell coal to Japan. If Burrard Inlet were able to handle all our other traffic, this would be good, but it is not able to do so. We have had plenty of evidence over the years that it is not.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
Surely we should attempt sooner or later to do a little for ourselves. I believe that Canada is a great nation and will someday acquire that stature in the nations of the world. The whole question of branch line abandonment deals specifically with costing. To me it is a matter of regret that when the Canadian transportation legislation was passed a few years ago we did not realize that these regulations would allow an appeal from that body to the Supreme Court. I know there is provision for appeal to the minister but I do not believe that the original intention was for appeal to the Supreme Court. This procedure could be detrimental in setting precedents which may not be wise in regard to transportation and costing. Railroad costing is a most complicated subject. The railroads have perfected a system which the Canadian Transport Commission did not accept completely.
Mr. Speaker, I hope the railroads lose their case in the Supreme Court. Having said that,
I believe we must examine the whole question of rail line abandonment from the point of view of need and subsidies and whether we can abandon rail lines holus-bolus without any regard for the necessity of the service even if it is losing money. It may be that there is provision for them to obtain a subsidy for loss incurred on a branch line. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that this whole question should receive exhaustive study and witnesses should be called, particularly from the CPR, before the transportation committee of this House.

I believe there are one or two differences, particularly in that part of the bill which relates to the financing of Air Canada, but the point I should like to make at the outset is that I think we should resist this business of being asked year after year to vote this money without being given any clear picture as to where we are going in this country in terms of a transportation policy.

Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada
I know, Mr. Speaker, that some of us have been rather critical of the number of reviews launched by this government. There seem to be many issues where we think action should be taken but instead we are getting reviews, studies, consideration and so on. But here is an area which does call for an over-all review before our whole transportation picture winds up in one awful mess. The fact that we are in danger of moving in the direction of an awful mess has been highlighted by the recent applications made by Canadian National Railways and Canadian Pacific Railway for the abandonment of most of their passenger services in this country.
May I say that few of us think that it would actually come to pass that passenger trains would cease to run in Canada. There is no sign that they will cease to run in the United States or Europe and other parts of the world, and it is terribly true that we do need passenger train services to help hold this country together.
I think it is clear what is taking place when an organization like Canadian Pacific Railway, parallelled by the Canadian National Railways, applies for permission to abandon passenger service. They are trying to get out of that part of the transportation business which is unprofitable in order to devote all their energies to those portions of the transportation business where they can make money.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
Some day the Government of Canada, and I do not know whether this government will do it, must look into the question of public versus private ownership in many fields, and in particular in the field of transportation. This government, in common with past Conservative governments, often pays tribute to the idea of public ownership up to a certain extent. They support public ownership where it is needed, but the record is clear that they do not really believe in it. They only bring it in when private enterprise is not able to fill the bill.
Here we have a proposition that transportation, which has many aspects including passenger service and freight service, air line service and all other related services that are tied into it can, in certain areas of our market economy, make money. So private enterprise wants to be in that part of the transportation business to make all the money it can out of freight traffic and those areas of transport that are profitable, and agrees to take on the

passenger services. Hon. members will remember the famous wording in the agreements of 1881 and in the Canadian Pacific Railway Act of 1881, which talked of that company providing railway service in Canada thereafter and for ever, which talked about perpetual operation and about service being provided in perpetuity. That is what organizations like the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and the other railways that eventually failed and had to be taken over as part of Canadian National Railways agreed to do in order to obtain a corner of our economy in which profits were to be made. Now, as the years have gone on, it turns out that no railway company in the world operating over any extended area makes a profit out of its passenger business; but there are profits to be made in freight and other portions of the transportation industry. So these organizations, these conglomerations that were prepared initially to promise service forever, want to get out of that part which is unprofitable but enjoy the gravy that is to be made in other sections of industry.
One can hardly blame these people too much for taking that view. That is the view private enterprisers take generally. But we of this party blame the government for not realizing that transportation is so basic and essential to the life of this country. We must resolve this issue. I think the government should change its stance, because it seems to be saying, "All right; we will subsidize private enterprisers in the unprofitable part of the operation. If necessary, we will take over the unprofitable part of the operation, but we will bend over backwards to make sure that private enterprisers are given every opportunity to make all the money they can out of the profitable sections of the industry."
In the case of Canadian National Railways, huge batches of figures and tables are thrust at us. My friend and colleague, the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters), has been reading some of the tables he obtained from the library. He asked me to explain them. I cannot explain them to him, nor can he explain them to me. Sometimes people say that we own Canadian National, but when I look at all the figures and the way the railway's debts are mounting, I think Canadian National owns us. The amount of our wealth we have to apportion to pay the interest on this ever-growing debt portends ill for the future. It is getting us nowhere.
Why is this done, Mr. Speaker? The reason is that this government wants to maintain a
November 13, 1969
regime under which the profitable parts of the transportation industry are left to private enterprise. Transportation must be looked at as a whole industry, and if our private enterprisers are not prepared to operate the industry as a whole in the spirit of the 1881 agreements entered into by the Canadian Pacific Railway and others, then the public should take the industry over as a whole.
As a result of pressures that the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Canadian National are exerting, the day will come-and it may not be far off-when a real threat to close down passenger lines will tie this country up far more than any industrial strike has ever tied it up. That will result in the government saying, "We must have passenger service, so we will take over that unprofitable part of the business and run it but we will let you fellows go on and retain the freight service; we will let private enterprise acquire more and more of the air line business and all those other services, the hotel, financial and other services that are part of the conglomerate known as the Canadian Pacific Company. Then we the government, we the people, we the taxpayers will pay the shot for that part which happens to be unprofitable."
Either these people are in the transportation business, or they are not. If they are in it, they should be obligated to run the whole of it. If they are not prepared to run the whole of it and give us the kind of service that has been promised over the years, then they should get out of it and let the Canadian people, through the well tried medium of public ownership, take it over and run it in their own interests.
Some people who do not like this kind of reasoning will say, "Are not we going to run ourselves into debt if we run the unprofitable part of the services?" Please note, I am saying that we should have the profitable parts as well as the unprofitable parts. Of course, some members of Parliament may say, "Maybe we should not run the part that is unprofitable." The truth is that all this is a piece of bookkeeping fiction, if I may call it that.
The running of passenger train services in the market place economy seems to produce a loss. But the country does not lose because we have passenger train services; the country does not lose because we are all tied together with these bands of steel. And now, of course, we have air line services and all the rest of it. The country does not lose because it costs money to maintain a postal service, and
Provision of Moneys to CNR and Air Canada because we have docks and wharves and roads and all sorts of services that we must provide socially because they cannot be provided either individually or on a profit-making basis. If, as no doubt we all agree, Canada needs and will continue to need a whole transportation industry, which includes railway passenger service, for a long time to come, I submit that this should be the responsibility of the government itself. I would not be doctrinaire and insist that we are not prepared to let our private enterprisers have their share of the industry if they want to take it over. But, no; they do not want it all. They want only the profitable parts and are prepared to let the rest of it be owned by the public. As the previous speaker pointed out, and I think we are all aware of this, both the major railways of this country have a record of downgrading their passenger services-particularly the Canadian Pacific Railway-so that people will not use them and rely on them. The railways then turn around and say it is costing them money, and that they need to be bailed out.

Something should be said about the bill of goods that was put over on us a few years ago when this arrangement was made for the 80 per cent subsidy on a loss. The railways can get this by applying for the right to discontinue passenger service. It seems now that we just built into the legislation an open challenge to these railways. It is strange how the one we do not own and the one we do own seem to work together. When one applies for abandonment, the other applies for abandonment, and so on. We seem to have built into our legislation a challenge to the railways to come along a few years later and apply for an 80 per cent subsidy, thereby putting us on the spot. They know the people of Canada, the Parliament and the government of this country realize we must have passenger service and if they threaten, as they do, to abandon it the government will pick up the tab or take over that service.
I speak as strongly as I can, Mr. Speaker, against moving in that direction. I refer not only to the direction of paying 80 per cent of the losses that these companies may designate but in the direction of taking over only the passenger operation and allowing this private enterprise outfit to carry on with the profit making part of the whole business. I submit if there is an area of our national life that calls for a review and an in-depth survey, it is this

It is because those in power today do not want to disturb this situation in which profits can be made on part of the industry. As for passenger service, it will not be allowed to drop because the country needs it. This is no way to run things. This is no way to talk of giving leadership or of accepting responsibility for the life of this country. I call upon this government not to just come along year after year with this bill and stand up and tell us in a seven minute speech that it is the same bill we had last year, the year before that, the year before that and the same bill we will probably have next year and the year after.
Surely transportation is important enough to the life of this country that we should analyse, review and resolve it in rational and sensible terms. I thought that was what we were going to get a few years ago when Mr. Pickersgill introduced that bill of his. He gave us a long preamble to the national transportation policy. It was a great speech. He made it clear that he was such an expert in the field that he was able to take the job provided by the bill, but of course that is all water under the bridge. I remember when he spoke I had the feeling that maybe the time had come when we were going to get a critical examination of the whole subject of transportation in our country. However, we did not get that. All we got was a reshuffling of the financial arrangements without changing the basic concept under which transportation is still operating, namely, let the private enterprise people have all the profit they can get from the profitable phases, and let them come to us crying poverty as far as the essential services are concerned and we will pay the deficit or take over the service. That, Mr. Speaker, is not good government.
When the Minister without Portfolio was proposing this bill I had the feeling it would be good if we had a Parliament with enough people in it with the guts to refuse to pass the bill.

We should not worry that the effect of any action we might take will result in the stopping of train service. The railways themselves are doing this. If we had a Parliament with enough people in it with the guts to say no to this kind of legislation and refuse to pass it, it might bring home to the government the realization that it has not examined transportation policy. The government does not have a policy that is good for the sixties, which are almost over, no policy for the seventies and certainly no policy for the final decades of this century. No one tried to impose that stricture at this time because the threats to cut out passenger service have brought the whole thing to a head in the minds of hon. members and the public. If we had a Parliament that would not pass this bill, the government might realize the jig is up and that they cannot go on perpetuating this mess. This is a completely unsatisfactory situation. We must resolve the whole transportation picture.
I want to say a word about the effect of this policy on the workers of the transportation industry. I come from a city which is a major centre for employees of Canadian National Railways and Canadian Pacific Railway. These employees have been going through a good deal of agony for the last decade or more, wondering what is happening as services are being cut one after the other. They are also wondering what is happening now. I submit that this is part of the responsibility of an industry such as the transportation industry. This industry has no moral right to talk about discontinuing these services without realizing what it can mean to those who

are working in the industry and who have helped to build it up to the strong, effective industry which it has been over the years. The government has no concern for these people.

My hon. friend and colleague asked where private enterprise was when Air Canada was starting out. I was here in 1944, I think it was, when the Right Hon. C. D. Howe brought in a measure having to do with air policy which resulted in the setting up of Air Canada as a completely publicly-owned corporation. I said 1944, but perhaps it was in 1945 or 1946-it was around there somewhere. Mr. Howe was asked why it had to be a completely publicly-owned proposition; why the others had not been let in. And he, the apostle of private enterprise, organizer, entrepreneur, pragmatist as he was, stood in his place and said he had tried his best to get the CPR to come in along with the CNR in joint ownership, but failed. This was in the middle forties at a time when there was nothing to be made out of it; the others did not want any part of it, so this great public set-up was the result.
Mr. Howe said, when some of us supported his move, that he intended to make the corporation so strong that nothing could be done by either its enemies or its friends-that was a crack at us-to upset it. But we all know what has happened since then. I realize I am rambling, I am reminiscing, but I think I am not far from the truth about this whole transportation system and its history in Canada for a full hundred years. We have never been able to sit down and look at transportation as being an essential service which the country needs and which should therefore be provided

Mr. Speaker, the other day during the question period I raised a question about the inequalities of salaries and employment advancement opportunities for the women of Canada who are employed in the federal public service. This question was inspired, if I might use that word, by a recent and excellent speech by Mr. Carson, chairman of the Public Service Commission of Canada. Possibly I did not phrase my question accurately enough to convey my real interest because the minister replied that he would be glad to send me a copy of Mr. Carson's speech. I did not consider that this was an adequate reply and I asked the minister whether he would consider taking a really serious look at the situation which is one that affects a great many women in Canada both in the public and private sector. This has been well outlined as far as our federal women employees are concerned by Mr. Carson.
I want to take advantage of the adjournment debate tonight to put a few more facts forward in illustration of what seems to be a need for a stepped-up effort on the part of our government to rid the employment service of this old and outworn prejudice against women in executive or foremost positions in the public service. Let me quote from the speech last week by Mr. Carson, the chairman of the Public Service Commission of Canada, in which he said:
In 1967 for example, almost 60 per cent of all men In the public service made less than $6,000 a year, but no less than 90 per cent of all women ... so employed were under that level.

He also states, as a result of a study undertaken on a comprehensive basis of men and women employed in the public service:
Our study has computed that a male has 100 times the chance of reaching an annual salary of $14,000 than does a female in the public service.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
I suggest these two quotations indicate that economic discrimination exists throughout the public service in respect of female employees. I am sure many people would agree with me when I suggest a similar prejudice exists in the private sector. I know, and I am sure the minister or whoever speaks tonight will say, that efforts are being made to meet the situation in the federal public service field and that the prejudice which involves women and retards their advancement to a higher salary or position is an intangible one. It is also said that this hangover from past ages has nothing to do with legislation. I agree, but I am sure the women across the country would agree with me when I say the federal authority in this field, representing the public of Canada, should be expected to give a lead in this regard and speed up efforts to correct the situation which prevails. If this is done, then I think the federal government will set an example for the rest of the country in accelerating the progress of women toward economic equality in our country at least so far as salary and employment are concerned.
In concluding my remarks I should like to remind hon. members that in reply to a question I asked in 1966 on a similar subject, the former prime minister, Mr. Pearson, at that time said unequivocally yes to me when I asked whether appointments to bodies such as the Atlantic Development Board, other boards, the Economic Council of Canada, the judiciary, the diplomatic corps and the CBC would be made by the government on the basis of a due proportion being filled by qualified women. Three years ago Mr. Pearson said yes on that particular point. We have yet to see any real action to back up that undertaking. I wish to say to the minister and others that we do appreciate that the chairman of the Public Service Commission is aware of the situation in the public service. I ask the minister to do everything possible in supporting the chairman of that commission and expediting equality for women in the employment service.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the hon. gentleman who has just spoken we subscribe both
November 13, 1969	COMMONS DEBATES
to the analysis and views expressed by the chairman of the Public Service Commission. I think this is an excellent analysis. As the hon. member suggests, we will do all that is reasonable to see that these hopes and aspirations are furthered. In quoting from one passage the hon. gentleman suggested, perhaps inadvertently, that there was inequality of salary between men and women, inequality in the sense that men on a quantitative basis draw higher salaries than women in the public service. Perhaps this carries the implication that women might be paid less than men for equivalent qualifications or equivalent jobs. I am sure he will appreciate this is not so. The law is quite explicit on this point. There is equal pay for equal work as between both sexes in the public service. There is no complaint on that score.
Apart from this I would be glad to say that, like Mr. Pearson, we want to see a greater participation by those of the fairer sex in the public service, and as the chairman of the Public Service Commission has indicated, he is conscious of the problems to be faced and is putting forth his best efforts to see that this proportion is increased.

OFFICIAL LANGUAGES-INCLUSION OF COST OF SCHOOL IN GRANT FOR BILINGUAL PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I asked the Secretary of State (Mr. Pelletier) today if the amount of $3 million earmarked for the building of the Civil Service School of Languages was included in the $50 million grant promised by the Federal Government for the bilingual programs.
I suggest this is an urgent question, because a great many Canadians are worried about the manner in which this amount of $50 million is going to be spent.
In view of the amount of money involved in learning a second language in Canada, this allocation of $3 million makes us wonder if the expenditures made in view of turning Canada into a bilingual country have been provided for or if the grant of $50 millions to bilingualism programs will be used also for the construction of language schools.
Speaking about Canadians' concern, a British Columbia citizen stated, and I shall quote an article published in Le Soleil of November 11th which was entitled: "The $50 millions from Ottawa should be used to improve the
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion condition of the French-speaking minorities in this country", and I quote:
We will have to see to it that the $50 millions Ottawa will contribute in order to promote bilingualism are not used by English-speaking provinces to help English-speaking Canadians to become bilingual but to improve the condition of their French-speaking minorities.
This is the view expressed last week-end by a British Columbia French-speaking visitor to Levis-
Mr. Romeo Paquette, secretary of the British Columbia French-Canadian Association, was speaking especially of his province-
[DOT] (10:20 p.m.)
At the present time there is no adequate machinery to ensure that the French Canadians will be properly represented on the school boards.
Mr. Paquette wonders how the French-speaking people in his province will be able to work towards self-determination if the institutions are English and if English-speaking people decide on the solutions to the problems of the French-speaking people.
If western citizens are concerned about the disposal of the $50 million made available to Canadians, Quebecers are also justified in being worried and in asking questions which urgently require answers.
According to Quebec Minister of Cultural Affairs, Quebec had told Ottawa that if it intended to provide technical and financial assistance, it would naturally have to consider the whole situation, namely the efforts Quebec had made to set up an educational system favourable both to the French and the English people.
He added, and I quote:
As for the premier, he concluded: In Toronto, the Education Minister (Mr. Davis) stated the government policy, at least some principles of the Ontario government, and he asked for retroactivity. If this has a retroactive effect, in Quebec, it will have to be for more than a hundred years.
All this, Mr. Speaker, to tell you that there is much to be done in the field of linguistic research, in order to do justice to everyone, because, in my opinion, individuals and peoples should not be judged according to how well they speak or write.
However, language remains, in my opinion, a privileged instrument for the moulding of the mind and character. A cripple or a sick person can be endowed with very lofty qualities. We must not conclude that physical disability is unimportant and that the spread of illness should be encouraged. To speak incorrectly and to write poorly is not only a discourtesy towards others, but a sin against oneself, according to Plato, who had nothing in common with a silly bluestocking or of a

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion man for whom hair styling and whiteness of teeth are more important than friendship and courage.
As for that specific inquiry directed to the minister concerning the manner in which the amount of $50 million will be spent, I would like to quote what a professor of Matane-a town located east of Quebec City-Mr. Via-teur Beaupre said, and I quote:
The quality of the language is closely connected with a people's economic and political life. It is certain that our present federalism seriously threatens our culture and our language because, as an increasingly centralizing magnet, despite our protests, it strives consciously and unconsciously to establish unity and uniformity. The English-speaking majority cannot but work to build the country in its image and transcendence. The melody is sung by English tenors; French Canadians, Eskimos and others are asked not to spoil the concert or to learn the right lyrics. If we want to sing our own song, they will tell us that we cannot carry a tune and must have faith in them because, they say, we are fond of your "Alouette, gentille alouette" and we promise it will be respected from coast to coast. On a single condition: that you shall not sing another song while we are teaching "Alouette" in the Prairies and Baffin Land.
But I will not insist on this aspect of the question, although it is of utmost importance. Whatever the political status of the province of Quebec, we will always have to make a gigantic effort to save the French language in North America. It will be saved or irreparably lost in a few years hence. And let there be firmly believed that if Ottawa proffers its hand, it is to grasp it later with both hands and compel us to follow its own dance. If we dance well, to the English rhythm, the French-Canadians outside the province of Quebec will be allowed to keep their folklore-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the answer to the first part of
DEBATES	November 13, 1968
the question of the hon. member is no. The cost of the Language Center of the Civil Service Commission located on Carson Road is paid from the budget of the Public Works Department.
The Department of Public Works bought the Saint-Jean Marie Vianney seminary last summer for $2,700,000. Renovations will bring the total cost to roughly $3 million by the end of the 1969-70 fiscal year.
The budget of the Public Service Commission provides for expenditures of $5,777,000 for language training in the year 1969-70. Operating expenses for the Centre are included in that amount.
With regard to the $50 million I mentioned here on November 6, that amount will be used to set up federal-provincial programs for the teaching of the minority language, that is the mother tongue of English minorities in Quebec, and of French minorities in the other provinces, and, as an adjunct to this, for the teaching of English and French as second tongue.
The hon. member may rest assured that the amount used for the purchase and the amount to be used for the operation of that new Public Service Commission Center were not taken out of the money voted towards the federal-provincial programs for the teaching of languages.
